content: Patients diagnosed with head and neck cancer frequently experience malnutrition. Surgical procedures for these cancers are often intricate and may follow a course of radiotherapy. Consequently, these patients are at risk of developing postoperative complications, including fistulae, wound infections, and systemic infections such as pneumonia. Enhancing nutritional support may be a potential strategy to improve recovery and reduce the likelihood of these complications. Specialized nutritional formulas, referred to as immunonutrition, contain not only basic nutrients but also specific components such as amino acids (e.g., arginine and glutamine), ribonucleic acid (RNA), and omega-3 fatty acids. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of immunonutrition compared to standard nutritional support on postoperative recovery in adult patients undergoing elective surgery for head and neck cancer. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared immunonutrition administered preoperatively, postoperatively, or perioperatively to standard polymeric nutritional supplements or no supplementation. The primary outcomes assessed were the length of hospital stay, wound infections, fistula formation, and adverse events related to feed tolerance. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality and other postoperative complications. A total of 19 RCTs involving 1,099 participants were included in the analysis. The participants' mean age ranged from 47 to 66 years. Most studies had fewer than 25 patients per treatment group, and the majority utilized immunonutrition formulas containing arginine, although the specific products, dosages, and duration of intervention varied. Follow-up periods for outcome assessment ranged from five days to 16 months or more. Regarding the primary outcomes: There was no evidence to suggest that immunonutrition reduced the length of hospital stay (mean difference: -2.5 days; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -5.11 to 0.12; 10 studies, 757 participants; low-quality evidence). Immunonutrition did not appear to significantly affect the risk of wound infections (risk ratio [RR]: 0.94; 95% CI: 0.70 to 1.26; 12 studies, 812 participants; very low-quality evidence). Fistula formation may be reduced with immunonutrition. The absolute risk of fistula formation was 11.3% in the standard care group compared to 5.4% in the immunonutrition group, with an RR of 0.48 (95% CI: 0.27 to 0.85; 10 studies, 747 participants; low-quality evidence). There was no evidence of a difference in feed tolerance or adverse events between the immunonutrition and control groups (RR: 1.33; 95% CI: 0.86 to 2.06; 9 studies, 719 participants; very low-quality evidence). For the secondary outcomes: There was no evidence of a difference in all-cause mortality between the groups (RR: 1.33; 95% CI: 0.48 to 3.66; 14 studies, 776 participants; low-quality evidence). Other postoperative complications, such as pneumonia and urinary tract infections, were infrequently reported. In conclusion, immunonutrition may reduce the risk of postoperative fistula formation in patients undergoing surgery for head and neck cancer. However, there was no evidence to support its effectiveness in improving other outcomes, such as length of hospital stay, wound infections, or all-cause mortality. The included studies were generally small and/or at high risk of bias, and the overall quality of evidence was judged to be low or very low. Further research involving larger, higher-quality studies is necessary to better understand the potential benefits of immunonutrition in this patient population.
